'''Kathryn Lee Emanuel Lawson''' (September 15, 1926 – September 25, 2008) was one of the first few female African American chemists who worked in [[Sandia National Laboratories]]. She studied properties of [[irradiated]] materials in [[Solid-state physics|Crystal Physics]] research division.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/1054399980|title=African American Women Chemists.|last=Brown, Jeannette.|date=2011|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=9780199909612|pages=111–114|oclc=1054399980}}</ref> She earned her PhD from the [[University of New Mexico]] in [[radiochemistry]] in 1957.<ref name=":1" />

== Early life and education ==
Katheryn Emanuel was born to John Venus Emanuel and Ida L. Gillispe in [[Shreveport, Louisiana|Shreveport]], Louisiana on September 15, 1926.<ref name=":1" /> After Emanuel attended racially segregated schools and graduated as the [[salutatorian]] of a racially segregated high school in 1941, she went to Dillard College (now [[Dillard University]]), a historically black college, in New Orleans and graduated with BA [[Cum laude|Cum Laude]] in [[Natural science|Natural Science]] in 1945.<ref name=":1" /> Two years later, Emanuel went to Tuskegee Institute (now [[Tuskegee University]]) to pursue master's degree in organic chemistry.<ref name=":1" /> Meanwhile, she served as an assistant professor of chemistry in multiple colleges, including [[Bishop College]], [[Savannah State University]], [[Talladega College]] and [[Grambling State University]], all of which are [[Historically black colleges and universities|historically black colleges]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Black Women Scientists in the United States|last=Warren|first=Wini|publisher=Indiana University Press|year=2000|isbn=0-253-33603-1|location=Bloomington|pages=[https://archive.org/details/blackwomenscient00warr/page/177 177-178]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/blackwomenscient00warr/page/177}}</ref>

Four years later, Emanuel got promoted to and worked as associate professor of chemistry at Central State College (a historically black college and now [[Central State University]]) in [[Wilberforce, Ohio]] until 1954.<ref name=":1" /> Emanuel was offered an assistantship and the opportunity to study for PhD in [[University of New Mexico]]. Lawson finished her PhD in [[radiochemistry]] with a dissertation of ''Behavior of Indium at Tracer Concentrations'' in 1957.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
Katheryn Emanuel Lawson started work as a [[biochemist]] in [[Veterans Administration Hospital]] in [[Albuquerque, New Mexico|Albuquerque]], New Mexico in 1957.<ref name=":1" /> A year later, she was invited to work in [[Sandia National Laboratories]] in [[Crystal physics|Crystal Physics]] Research Division. At that time, Sandia Labs needed PhD graduates to work on weapon development.<ref name=":1" /> Lawson worked in material research while her job was to analyze molecular structure of irradiated materials.<ref name=":1" /> She also studied optical properties of [[Transition metal|transition metals]] and their combination with other elements. She tested their electrical and magnetic properties, which helped prove [[Crystal field theory|Crystal Field Theory]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite magazine |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Nd4DAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA67 |title=Science Couple Finds Success In Albuquerque |magazine=[[Ebony (magazine)|Ebony]] |publisher=Johnson Publishing Company |issn=0012-9011 |volume=20 |number=8 |pages=67–73 |date=June 1965 |access-date=2019-07-25 |via=Google Books}}</ref>

While at Sandia National Labs, Lawson successively published several papers and books throughout her career. Her works include ''Behavior of carrier-free tracers'',<ref>Kahn, M., Lawson, K. Emanuel., Jones, K. B., Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory., U.S. Atomic Energy Commission. (1960). ''Behavior of carrier-free tracers: (a bibliography of unclassified references).'' Albuquerque: University of New Mexico.</ref> ''Infrared absorption of inorganic substances''<ref>Lawson, Katheryn Emanuel. ''Infrared Absorption of Inorganic Substances''. New York: Reinhold, 1961.</ref> and ''Ion-exchange resins, a bibliography of unclassified references,''<ref>Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory, et al.. Ion-exchange Resins, a Bibliography of Unclassified References. Los Alamos, N.M.: Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory of the University of California, 1957.</ref>  and thermal properties of protective materials.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Lawson|first=Katheryn|date=1997|title=Effects of Porosity in Graphite Materials on Ablation in Arc-Heated Jets|url=https://arc.aiaa.org/doi/abs/10.2514/3.27954?journalCode=jsr|journal=J. Spacecraft|volume=14|pages=19–24|doi=10.2514/3.27954|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In 1965, she was featured with her husband Kenneth Lawson in [[Ebony (magazine)|''Ebony Magazine'']].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

Later in her career, she committed to [[National Urban League]]'s Black Executive Exchange Program to advise young African American to pursue higher education and to advise white manager to accept and recommend them.<ref name=":1" /> She also served on Fair Housing Board in Albuquerque after 1963.<ref name=":2" />

Lawson also worked at [[Bendix Corporation]] Research Labs in [[Southfield, Michigan|Southfield, M]]I, starting in the 1970s.<ref name=":3" />

She was a member of [[American Chemical Society]].<ref name=":2" />

== Personal life ==
Katheryn Emanuel Lawson married Kenneth Lawson, who was a chemist-bacteriologist studying for PhD in [[University of New Mexico]], in 1954.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> The couple had two sons, William, who was born when she was in graduate school, and Kenneth Jr.<ref name=":1" />  Lawson died in [[Farmington, Michigan]] on September 25, 2008.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":0" />
